text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: each member starts with 20 tokens, where keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75, while putting a token in the group account seems to yield 0.75 to each member, likely including myself, based on the standard public goods game setup.

So keeping tokens private is individually dominant since 1 > 0.75 regardless of what others do, yet full cooperation (everyone contributing everything) produces a better outcome for the group overall. This creates the classic tension between individual rationality and collective welfare, which matters for how I should think about strategy across the 10 rounds.

Defecting individually gains only 0.25 per token while costing the rest of the group 2.25 per token, so the socially efficient and signaling-friendly choice is clear. Given it's round one and the goal is group-level, I'll contribute the full 20 to the group account.

I'm setting up the formula for my own payoff based on how many tokens I keep versus contribute, factoring in everyone else's choices too.

Working through the algebra, I find that each token I contribute only costs me 0.25 net personally but gives 1.5 points to each other member — meaning contributing is socially efficient overall (total gain of 5.25 points per token versus -2.25 for hoarding), even though individually keeping tokens is still more profitable for me alone.

So the dominant strategy for a selfish individual is to keep everything, since one point beats 0.75. Yet if everyone instead cooperates and contributes all tokens, everyone ends up with 105 points each versus just 20 if everyone keeps — a classic public goods dilemma where individual rationality undermines the collective outcome.

With 10 rounds and no real punishment mechanism besides reciprocity, backward induction suggests defection could unravel cooperation, but I lean toward starting with a generous contribution to signal cooperative intent and see how others respond.
